title: Minimum Moves to Reach Target with Rotations
description: Move and rotate a 2-cell snake across a grid to a target position, using BFS over an (anchor, orientation) state space.

sections.title: Minimum Moves to Reach Target with Rotations

content.title: Minimum Moves to Reach Target with Rotations

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

An n x n grid has 0 for empty cells and 1 for obstacles. A snake occupies 2 cells, starting horizontally at (0,0) and (0,1). In one move, the snake can move right, move down, or rotate clockwise (switching between horizontal and vertical), as long as the cells it moves into or sweeps through during rotation are empty and within bounds. Return the minimum number of moves to reach the target, horizontal, occupying (n-1, n-2) and (n-1, n-1). Return -1 if impossible.

blocks.caption: BFS over (anchor cell, orientation) states finds the shortest sequence of slides and rotations.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Grid","n x n, 0 (empty) or 1 (obstacle)"],["Start","Horizontal, occupying (0,0) and (0,1)"],["Target","Horizontal, occupying (n-1,n-2) and (n-1,n-1)"],["Moves","Right, down, or rotate clockwise, all requiring the swept cells to be clear"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Minimum moves to reach a target configuration is BFS, but the snake's configuration is more than just a single cell: it needs an anchor position AND an orientation (horizontal or vertical). This is another instance of expanding the BFS state beyond raw position, this time adding a discrete orientation flag rather than a numeric budget.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Similar in spirit to Shortest Path with Alternating Colors, where the state needed an extra dimension (there, required edge color; here, snake orientation) beyond plain position.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a 2-cell-long rigid piece navigating a maze, like sliding a domino. It can slide right or down as a whole, or pivot 90 degrees around its head, but a pivot sweeps through a 2x2 area, so all 4 cells of that area must be clear, not just the 2 the piece is moving into.

blocks.caption: A rotation pivots around the head, sweeping a 2x2 area that must be fully clear.

items: Represent state as (anchor row, anchor col, orientation), where the anchor is the top-left of the snake's 2 occupied cells.
Horizontal at (r,c) occupies (r,c) and (r,c+1); vertical at (r,c) occupies (r,c) and (r+1,c).
A rotation from horizontal to vertical (or back) requires the OTHER two cells of the 2x2 block, not just the destination cells, to be clear and in bounds.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
A 3x3 empty grid (no obstacles). Start (0,0) horizontal, target (2,1) horizontal.

blocks.content: {"headers":["BFS layer","States reached (row, col, orientation)"],"rows":[["1","(1,0,H) via move down, (0,0,V) via rotate"],["2","(1,1,H), (2,0,H), (1,0,V), (0,1,V), (0,0,H)"],["3","reaches (2,1,H), the target"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The target is first reached at BFS layer 3, matching a hand-traceable path: move right to (0,1,H), move down to (1,1,H), move down to (2,1,H). A blocked variant where the target cells themselves are obstacles correctly returns -1, since the target state can never be validly reached.
5. How Should We Think?

A brute-force BFS explores this same state space but recomputes each move's validity from scratch inline within the transition logic, which is already reasonably efficient; the real risk is getting the rotation validity condition wrong (checking only the destination cells instead of the full swept 2x2 area).

The optimized version is the same BFS, processed strictly layer by layer so the step count is implicit, with the target check performed at generation time (the moment a new state is produced) rather than only when dequeued, avoiding one unnecessary extra layer.
6. Brute Force Solution
BFS over (row, col, orientation) states using a general visited set, checking for the target only when a state is dequeued.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","At most 2 orientations per cell, each visited once"],["Space","O(n^2)","Visited array plus the BFS queue"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This approach is already asymptotically optimal for this problem; the main refinement below is a small efficiency and clarity improvement, not a different complexity class.
8. Optimize the Solution

Process the BFS queue strictly layer by layer, and check whether a newly generated state IS the target the moment it is produced, returning immediately. This avoids storing a distance value in each queue entry and returns as early as possible within the correct BFS layer.

items: A 3D boolean array visited[row][col][orientation] gives O(1) state lookups.
For each state, generate valid moves: slide right/down (if the destination cells are clear), and rotate (if the OTHER two cells of the swept 2x2 block are clear).
Check the target condition immediately when a new state is generated, returning the current layer count.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A multi-cell object's configuration (position plus orientation) becomes the BFS state, not just a single cell.
A rotation that sweeps through cells needs ALL swept cells validated, not just the final destination cells.
This state-expansion pattern (position plus an extra discrete or numeric dimension) recurs across nearly every "harder" grid BFS problem in this category.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Minimum Moves to Reach Target with Rotations is solved with BFS over (anchor position, orientation) states. Sliding moves check the destination cells, while rotation moves check the full swept 2x2 area, and the first BFS layer reaching the target orientation and position gives the minimum number of moves, all in O(n^2) time.
